title: Everyday mysticism
hookLine: Karl Rahner said the Christian of the future would be a mystic or nothing
tomorrow: For the life of the world

lines: A MYSTIC, OR NOTHING AT ALL.
cards: Who counts as a mystic? Saints with visions. Hermits in caves.
People who seem to float a little above the rest of us. Karl Rahner, a German Jesuit priest and theologian, gave a different answer.

He's remembered for saying, in effect, that the Christian of the future will be a mystic, or will not be anything at all. That sounds like an impossibly high bar, until you hear what he meant by mystic.
A new week starts here, in an ordinary place.

teach.h: A MYSTIC: ONE WHO HAS EXPERIENCED GOD.
teach.b: For Rahner, a mystic isn't someone with visions. He means someone who has actually experienced God, not only heard about God secondhand.

Faith that rests on custom alone, he thought, would struggle in a world where custom no longer carries people along. So where would ordinary people meet God? Not mainly in rare moments, Rahner said, but inside daily life.
Keeping silent when you've been wronged and could defend yourself. Forgiving when no one will thank you for it. Doing what your conscience asks when no one will ever know.
Staying faithful in a task that brings no reward and no feeling of glory. In moments like that, he said, a person may be touching the Spirit at work, even if it feels like nothing at all.
The letter to the Colossians, speaking about ordinary household work, says something close: "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men."
If that's so, the kitchen, the commute and the office aren't outside God. Rahner's name for this was a mysticism of everyday life.

teach.h: NOT A LADDER OUT, A WAY IN.
teach.b: Not a ladder out of the ordinary. A way down into it. Others have said it in their own words.
Brother Lawrence, the Carmelite lay brother this path met earlier, worked in the kitchen and spoke of practicing the presence of God among the pots and pans.
The vocabulary differs, and the direction is the same: the plain moment may be the place.

how: Some Christians end the day by looking back for where God was present in ordinary events, a practice known in Jesuit spirituality as the examen; others speak of practicing the presence of God in daily work.

o: seeing visions of saints while doing household chores
meeting God inside plain daily life, not rare visions
a secret practice handed only to advanced monks

p: whatsoever ye do, do it heartily
the presence of God among the pots

s: for Rahner, a mystic is someone who sees visions
he means someone who has actually experienced God, often in plain moments.
Rahner pointed to forgiving without thanks as a place God may be met
along with keeping silent when wronged, and doing right when no one will know.
Colossians says only religious tasks are done as to the Lord
"whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men."

games.q: a coworker takes credit for your work in a meeting. you could set the record straight, loudly. no one would ever know if you let it go. what does Rahner point to?
o: defend yourself in front of everyone.
keep silent and forgive, with no one noticing.
games.why: Rahner names moments like this, keeping silent when wronged and forgiving without thanks, as places a person may touch the Spirit, even when it feels like nothing.

practice: Look back over the last day for one ordinary moment that held something more: a time you held your tongue, a kindness nobody saw, a task finished well with no one watching.
Don't judge whether it counts; just stay with it and notice what was there. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for that moment; if you don't, simply let it be noticed.

wordCard.voice: Everyday mysticism. Karl Rahner's idea that God can be met inside daily life itself: in silence, in forgiveness, in faithfulness no one sees.

orig.note: Greek, Colossians 3:23: from the soul. the King James renders it "heartily": "whatsoever ye do, do it heartily."

carryVoice: Your line: mystic in the ordinary. No visions required, just a plain moment. Rest well.
